pumac-2007-geometry-a-06.title: Search over the lattice points on the sphere
pumac-2007-geometry-a-06.body:
The vertices are integer points with $x^2+y^2+z^2=85$. Since $85=81+4+0=49+36+0$ are its only representations, these are the $48$ points obtained from $(9,2,0)$ and $(7,6,0)$ by permuting coordinates and changing signs. The volume of the tetrahedron on four such points is $\frac16|\det(b-a,c-a,d-a)|$; checking all $\binom{48}4$ choices gives a maximum of $392$.

It is attained by $(-7,-6,0),(0,6,-7),(0,6,7),(7,-6,0)$: with $a=(-7,-6,0)$, $b-a=(7,12,-7)$, $c-a=(7,12,7)$, $d-a=(14,0,0)$, the determinant is $14\cdot(12\cdot7+7\cdot12)=2352$ and the volume is $\frac{2352}6=392$.

**Answer: 392**

pumac-2007-geometry-a-07.title: Art gallery theorem
pumac-2007-geometry-a-07.body:
This is Chvatal's art gallery problem: a polygon with $N$ vertices can always be guarded by $\lfloor N/3\rfloor$ points, and this many are sometimes necessary.

*Sufficiency.* Triangulate the polygon with diagonals and $3$-colour the vertices so each triangle has all three colours. The least-used colour appears at most $\lfloor N/3\rfloor$ times, and guards at those vertices see every triangle, hence the whole polygon.

*Necessity.* A "comb" with $\lfloor N/3\rfloor$ spikes needs a separate guard in each spike.

With $N=2007$: $\lfloor2007/3\rfloor=669$.

**Answer: 669**

pumac-2007-geometry-a-08.title: Symmetry and integration
pumac-2007-geometry-a-08.body:
The region is symmetric under $x\leftrightarrow y$ and the sign changes, so it consists of $8$ congruent pieces; take the piece $0\le y\le x$. The ellipses meet on $y=x$ where $4x^2=4$, so at $x=1$. In this piece the binding constraint is $3x^2+y^2\le4$, i.e. $x\le\sqrt{\frac{4-y^2}{3}}$, for $0\le y\le1$.

$$\text{piece}=\int_0^1\left(\sqrt{\tfrac{4-y^2}3}-y\right)dy=\frac1{\sqrt3}\left(\frac{\sqrt3}{2}+\frac{\pi}{3}\right)-\frac12=\frac{\pi}{3\sqrt3}.$$
(using $\int_0^1\sqrt{4-y^2}dy=\frac{\sqrt3}2+\frac\pi3$.) The total area is $\frac{8\pi}{3\sqrt3}=\frac{8\sqrt3\pi}{9}\approx4.84$.

**Answer: $\frac{8\pi}{3\sqrt3}$**

pumac-2007-geometry-a-09.title: Circumradius of the regular tetrahedron
pumac-2007-geometry-a-09.body:
The centres of the four unit spheres form a regular tetrahedron of edge $2$; its circumradius is $\frac{\sqrt6}{4}\cdot2=\frac{\sqrt6}2$. The fifth sphere is centred at the tetrahedron's centre (by symmetry) and touches each unit sphere externally, so its radius $r$ satisfies $r+1=\frac{\sqrt6}2$:
$$r=\frac{\sqrt6}2-1=\frac{\sqrt6-2}2\approx0.2247<1.$$
(The other tangent sphere, centred at the same point but touching internally, would have radius $\frac{\sqrt6}2+1>1$.)

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt6-2}2$**

pumac-2007-geometry-a-10.title: Power of a point from B and C
pumac-2007-geometry-a-10.body:
Let $a=BC$, $b=CA$, $c=AB$ and $BP=kc$, $CQ=kb$. From $MP\parallel AC$: $\frac{BM}{BA}=\frac{BP}{BC}=\frac{kc}a$, so $BM=\frac{kc^2}{a}$. From $NQ\parallel AB$: $CN=\frac{kb^2}{a}$.

The power of $B$ with respect to the circle gives $BM\cdot BA=BP\cdot BQ$:
$$\frac{kc^3}a=kc\,(a-kb)\ \Rightarrow\ kb=a-\frac{c^2}{a}=\frac{a^2-c^2}{a}.$$
The power of $C$ gives $CN\cdot CA=CQ\cdot CP$: $\frac{kb^3}a=kb(a-kc)\Rightarrow kc=\frac{a^2-b^2}{a}$.

Dividing, $\frac bc=\frac{a^2-c^2}{a^2-b^2}$, i.e. $b(a^2-b^2)=c(a^2-c^2)$, i.e. $a^2(b-c)=b^3-c^3=(b-c)(b^2+bc+c^2)$. Since $AB\ne AC$, $b\ne c$ and $a^2=b^2+bc+c^2$. Comparing with the law of cosines $a^2=b^2+c^2-2bc\cos A$ gives $\cos A=-\frac12$, so $\angle BAC=120^\circ$.

(Such triangles exist, e.g. $b=2,c=1,k=3/\sqrt7$; one checks the five points are concyclic.)

**Answer: $120^\circ$**
